name: Chloral hydrate
metabolism: Chloral hydrate is rapidly broken down by the liver, erythrocytes and other tissues to its active metabolite trichloroethanol; the reduction is catalysed by alcohol dehydrogenase and other enzymes. Trichloroethanol has a plasma time in the body of about 4 to 12 hours (1 to 2 days in neonates). A small but variable amount of chloral hydrate and a larger portion of trichloroethanol are oxidised to trichloroacetic acid (an inactive metabolite) in the liver and kidneys, and trichloroethanol may also be conjugated to trichloroethanol glucuronide. Chloral hydrate is not excreted unchanged in urine; metabolites are slowly excreted in urine, and some also into bile and faeces.
summary: Chloral hydrate is a sedative-hypnotic geminal diol first used in the 1870s. It was later replaced by safer and more effective alternatives, although it remained in use in the United States until at least the 1970s.
